author: Song Yu-jeong
title: The Memory Bookshop
text:
I hated winter. The cold air at daybreak, the nights that stretched on forever, the temperatures that dipped into negative like my moods, the biting winds that kept me trapped indoors. In winter, I was a bear in hibernation. All I wanted was to curl up in my dark cave.

Hmm, but should I go out for a walk today? I thought about an article I’d read online recently about the Inuit people. When they’re angry, they like to walk the emotion out of their system, and when the anger finally dissipates, the walk back serves as one of repentance and forgiveness. I liked that idea. So, I changed into one of the few winter outfits I owned and left the apartment. Behind me, the door shut with a heavy clang.

I’d moved to this apartment just before winter, so I hadn’t yet had the opportunity to properly explore the neighbourhood. I let my feet guide me forward. With my hands stuffed into the pockets of my thick padded jacket, I puffed out clouds of white smoke as I kept walking.

The biting winds threatened to slice my skin, and I hunched forward involuntarily. I thought back to that day when I’d visited the clinic and thrown the medicine into the dustbin.

Of course, we take time to process death. But seven years? You’ve been grieving for too long. You should be way past that stage by now.

The doctor’s words rose up in my mind. Time had chugged sluggishly outside his room while I made the payment, arranged the next appointment, and sat down in the waiting area to receive my medication. It was as if someone had deliberately held time hostage. The digits on my phone screen seemed to freeze. Everyone else had left. Just as my patience was about to run out, the clinic door swung open and a man rushed in.

Panting, he strode past the reception desk and barged into the doctor’s room. However, he must have found it empty. I was the last registered patient for the day, and even though consultation hours weren’t quite over, the doctor had left.

‘Excuse me, is there anyone here? Hey!’

The man’s face turned an ugly shade of purple as he yelled in the direction of the dispensary behind the reception desk.

The next moment, he stood stock-still and checked the watch on his left wrist. Tick tock, tick tock. The man’s eyes darted nervously, and I could almost hear the anxious ticks in my ears. He touched the watch as if it was a precious treasure. In contrast to the frayed blue leather strap, its polished face gleamed in the light.

‘Hey! Help! Someone’s dying!’ the man screamed in the direction of the dispensary.

Someone’s dying.

He probably said it in a fit of anger and frustration, but the words jolted me. An unnatural ringing filled my ears as the ground seemed to warp and surge like sloshing waves. I closed my eyes and shook my head – my defence mechanism whenever I felt a panic attack coming on.

What was happening?

‘Please … help …’

The minute hand on the wall clock ticked forward. At the sight, the man bit his lip and fell into silence. Although he was right in front of me, I had a curious feeling that he and I were in two separate dimensions. An absolute stillness pressed down on the waiting room.

‘Kim Jiwon-nim. Your medicine is ready.’

As the man slumped down in front of the reception desk, the nurse came out of the dispensary. I stood, inched past the man – avoiding his vacant eyes – took the medicine envelope, and fled the clinic.

My heart pounded in my chest and the pills rustled in the bag as I walked down the stairs. The consultation had barely lasted five minutes, but everything else had eaten up too much time. I’d never felt such strong regret over wasted time.

The doctor’s clinical attitude and the man’s vacant eyes flashed through my mind. And, as if it was the most natural thing to do, I chucked the bag of medicine into the next rubbish bin by the roadside.

Three weeks passed. In that time, I paid the price of suffering through more sleepless nights. But in moments of doubt, I conjured memories of the bulging medicine envelope, the unpleasant conversation with the doctor, and the man who’d rushed in frantically to the clinic. Maybe what I really needed wasn’t the pills or their chemical compounds.

Whoosh. A sharp gust of wind cuffed me by the ear. I shook my head, trying to snap out of the reverie. Something landed on my shoulder with a splat. It was raining. The grey light wasn’t just the winter gloom but the overcast clouds. The sudden downpour didn’t feel particularly welcoming now that I was outdoors without an umbrella. I held up my hands to make a useless shelter and ran under the nearest awning. The rain brought along a frigid cold and my teeth chattered.

‘Oh God … nothing’s going my way.’

I stood like a wet mouse under the awning. I thought I was hanging in there, but the world with its rain and cold and dark memories kept nudging me towards the precipice, as if I could never escape the fate of stumbling, falling, breaking, shattering. The rain hit my skin, but it felt like a gaping hole had opened in my heart, letting the wind in from all directions.

Someone’s dying!

Was this how the man at the clinic had felt? His desperate cries reverberated in my ears. What had caused his deep despair? I shook the droplets off my clothes and hair, as if they were the oppressive thoughts in my mind.

Thud, thud. The raindrops pelted down like bullets. I looked up and realized that I wasn’t standing below a vinyl awning but a rusty slate roof. The wooden deck beneath my feet was chipped in several places. I surveyed my surroundings. The single-storey building, an uncommon sight these days, looked dated. Grimy metal bars covered the opaque glass windows. On the rickety door was an OPEN sign.
